abstract_or_notes: Epigenetic Mechanisms of Human Adaptation to High-Background Radiation Introduction Epigenetics plays a significant role in enabling humans to biologically adapt to environments with elevated background radiation. In certain regions of the world – such as Kerala (India), Ramsar (Iran), and Yangjiang (China) – natural radiation levels far exceed normal background, yet local populations do not show corresponding increases in radiation-induced illnesses or genetic damage. This paradox suggests that adaptive responses have developed, allowing human cells to tolerate chronic low-dose ionizing radiation. Crucially, this adaptation appears to occur not through new DNA mutations, but through changes in gene regulation. abstract_or_notes: Investigating Chronic Low-Dose Radiation Mechanisms via Microbial Models Introduction Chronic low-dose ionizing radiation (IR) exposure poses a unique challenge to human health research. Unlike acute high-dose exposures, small sustained doses can quietly induce DNA lesions, oxidative stress, and subtle regulatory changes over long periods 1 2 . Yet ethical and practical constraints limit direct human or animal experimentation under chronic low-dose conditions.
